How Obama appointee and Trump nemesis Boasberg ended up overseeing Ilhan Omar warrant, other key cases

Judge James Boasberg oversees the Ilhan Omar search warrant fight, deportation flights, and California voter rolls, raising assignment questions.

Actual Article Body:
This material may not be published, broadcast, rewritten, or redistributed. ©2026 FOX News Network, LLC. All rights reserved. Quotes displayed in real-time or delayed by at least 15 minutes. Market data provided by Factset. Powered and implemented by FactSet Digital Solutions. Legal Statement. Mutual Fund and ETF data provided by LSEG.

Former DOJ prosecutor Jim Trusty joins 'America's Newsroom' to analyze the federal raid on Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington, D.C., home. Trusty discusses the DOJ search warrant executed by Homeland Security Investigations and reviews potential immigration charges.

Federal Judge James Boasberg, dubbed a "Radical left lunatic" by President Donald Trump, is presiding over several high-profile cases challenging actions made by the Trump administration, raising questions about how judges are assigned to cases.

The scrutiny comes as Boasberg, an Obama-appointed chief judge of the Washington, D.C., district court, oversees a challenge brought by several media outlets seeking to force the Justice Department to unseal the search warrant on the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn.

"Judge James Boasberg is now involved with the Ilhan Omar case," Steve Ferguson, a self-described business owner with more than 250,000 followers on X, wrote in a social media post. "Is everything rigged?"

In the federal court of the District of Columbia, cases are assigned to judges randomly by an electronic system managed by the clerk's office operating under the direction of the Calendar and Case Management Committee, according to the rules of the court. The committee consists of three to five judges appointed by the chief justice.

FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION

Judge Boasberg (Getty)

There are exceptions to the random-assignment process. For example, criminal grand jury matters are assigned to and overseen by the chief judge, currently Boasberg. This means Boasberg’s assignment to oversee the fight over unsealing the search warrant for Omar was "not a surprise" to Eric Wessan, Iowa’s solicitor general.

"But there are a lot of cases that seem to be going to judges maybe based on those cases having similarities, which is not what the local rules say," Wessan told Fox News Digital.

When a case needs to be reassigned, the Calendar and Case Management Committee will determine how the reassignment is made.

Wessan suggested that concerns over how case assignments are made are valid, considering some of the high-profile cases against the Trump administration which have appeared in Boasberg's docket.

"If one is just following anecdotally, there does seem to be a lot of high-profile cases in front of judges that seem to be expressing unusual amounts of frustration or disagreement with the administration," Wessan said, urging greater transparency in how case assignments are made.

TRUMP’S FIGHT OVER RARELY USED 18THCENTURY DEPORTATION LAW LIVES ON IN LATEST COURT CLASH

Federal law enforcement agents confront anti-ICE protesters during a demonstration outside the Bishop Whipple Federal Building in Minneapolis Jan. 15, 2026. (Getty Images)

The fight over unsealing the release of Omar's search warrant is just one of several cases involving the Trump administration and now on Boasberg's docket. Boasberg is also overseeing California’s lawsuit against the Trump administration over voter roll disputes.

On Friday, he ordered the administration to provide the state with the names and supporting information for roughly 20,000 people whom the DOJ claims are noncitizens on California’s voter rolls by the end of the day.

Boasberg has issued several consequential rulings against the Trump administration, including a high-profile March 2025 order directing the administration to turn around deportation flights carrying alleged Venezuelan gang members to El Salvador. The Trump administration fought against the order, pointing to the Alien Enemies Act as legal justification for the deportations.

The dispute over the administration’s use of the Alien Enemies Act eventually reached the Supreme Court, which vacated Boasberg's temporary restraining order blocking deportation flights, ruling that the case was brought in the wrong jurisdiction.

That same month, Boasberg was assigned a lawsuit seeking to preserve Signal messages after top Trump administration officials discussed plans for a Yemen strike in a group chat that accidentally included Atlantic editor-in-chief Jeffrey Goldberg. The judge later ordered the administration to preserve the messages.

The string of cases prompted Reps. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio; Darrell Issa, R-Calif.; and Chip Roy, R-Texas, to send a letter in May 2025 to the court clerk asking for greater clarity on how judicial assignments are made. The lawmakers questioned whether assignments were truly random as the court’s rules state.

"The Committee cannot independently verify the randomness of case assignments because the composition of assignment decks is kept secret," the lawmakers wrote.

"We must understand the nature of the case assignment process in the District Court — which is considering a number of cases challenging the Trump Administration’s policy decisions — to consider and develop appropriate legislation."

Venezuelan migrants flown from Guantanamo Bay via Honduras walk up a ladder after arriving on a deportation flight at Simon Bolivar International Airport in Maiquetia, La Guaira State, Venezuela, Feb. 20, 2025. (Reuters/Leonardo Fernandez Viloria)

FEDERAL JUDGE KICKED OFF 'BOTCH JOB' ANTI-DEI CASE AFTER STUNNING APPEALS COURT REBUKE

Meanwhile, Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., introduced legislation in July that would require federal district courts to assign cases randomly, without exceptions, naming it the Boasberg Act. The bill is stalled in committee.

"Judge Boasberg is the poster child for a rogue judge and exposed serious loopholes in our judicial system. Randomly assigning cases among judges ensures the American people can have confidence in the impartiality of our courts," Schmitt said in a statement.

Under the rules of the D.C. Court, the chief justice does not have the power to reassign a case. The Calendar and Case Management Committee handles case reassignments. The court must notify the judges and attorneys involved, but it does not have to publicly explain why a case was reassigned. Wessan has called for greater transparency.

"The rules shouldn’t say one thing if it’s not true. But if it is true, they could just say so. I think the issue is with the exceptions. What happens in those exceptional cases and how often do they occur?" Wessan said.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Given the frequency of the concerning episodes in the district court, erring on the side of transparency is probably prudent to the extent that there are exceptions to the normal random-assignment system."

Trump pleads for voters to pick Blakeman to save New York from ‘worst governor’

President Donald Trump endorsed Bruce Blakeman for New York governor during a tele-rally, calling incumbent Gov. Kathy Hochul the state's "worst governor."

Actual Article Body:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

See more of our coverage in your search results.

President Donald Trump on Saturday made a last-minute plea to New Yorkers to vote for Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman on Election Day, saying the Nassau County executive can save the Empire State from Gov. Kathy Hochul’s “failed and incompetent” leadership.

“Kathy Hochul may be the worst governor in the history of New York State and one of the worst in the nation,” roared the commander-in-chief during a tele-rally promoting the campaigns of Blakeman and two other New York Republicans, Attorney General candidate Saritha Komatireddy and upstate congressional hopeful Anthony Constantino.

“She been a disaster, and I can tell you that Bruce has been a friend of mine for a long time,” Trump added.

“Anybody that can do what he did in politics and get resounding results, and not only that, he has the safest county in the United States of America [according to US News & World Report] … He’s a great manager.”

Despite recent polls showing Hochul ahead anywhere from 11 to 14 points, Trump said he expects the Nassau County executive to win.

“I’ll be waiting for his call,” the president said. “I bet he’s going to be one of the first calls if he wins, and he’ll get tremendous help from the federal government. And it’s hard to help people that do such a bad job. It’s almost like throwing good money after bad.”

Hochul spokesperson Ryan Radulovack responded by attempting to paint Trump as a boogeyman, something the governor has also done many times throughout the campaign.

“Blakeman … started with the promise to ‘bring Trump-style leadership to Albany,’ and his closing message is telling people how little he regrets going full Trump in this campaign,” added Radulovack.

“Gov. Hochul has put money back in New Yorkers’ pockets, invested $4 billion in public safety, and fought back against Trump’s attacks,” while Blakeman “defends everything Trump does.”

Trump during the tele-rally also found some time to claim that the war with Iran is all but over.

“We’re winning very easily the war with Iran,” Trump said.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Trump rips ex-lawyer Alina Habba’s ‘obnoxious’ $50M deal with pardoned Venezuelan banker’s family

"I thought it was totally obnoxious and outrageous, and it's not acceptable. Not acceptable at all."

Actual Article Body:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

See more of our coverage in your search results.

President Trump tore into his former personal attorney Alina Habba on Saturday night, calling her reported $50 million contract with the family of a Venezuelan banker he later pardoned “totally obnoxious and outrageous.”

“I thought it was terrible,” Trump told reporters as he arrived at a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida, where he joked he had come dressed as himself.

The president said he told Habba he didn’t want her to be paid.

“You know, it’s one thing for a person to get paid legal fees or whatever. She’s a lawyer,” Trump said. “I thought it was totally obnoxious and outrageous, and it’s not acceptable. Not acceptable at all.”

The family of Julio Herrera Velutini guaranteed Habba more than $50 million over four years in exchange for serving as general counsel of Concord Partners, a family company registered just days before she signed on, the New York Times reported last week.

Herrera, a billionaire banker, once faced federal bribery charges. By August 2025, his case had been whittled down to a guilty plea on a single misdemeanor campaign finance violation instead.

The family put Habba on a princely retainer of $10 million a year, plus bonuses, according to the Times. The 42-year-old attorney teed the job up while she was still on the Justice Department’s payroll.

Habba was just two weeks into her new gig at Concord Partners when Trump pardoned her boss’ father.

The lawyer, for her part, insists the timing is pure happenstance.

“Any insinuation that my employment — all of which has been vetted and disclosed to the DOJ — had anything to do with securing a pardon is false,” Habba told the Times.

The White House has also denied any connection, the outlet reported.

Trump “erupted” when he learned of the contract, according to the Times, then told aides and allies that some of the money ought to find its way to his future presidential library or some other Trump-linked outfit.

On Saturday, the president said he didn’t necessarily expect Habba herself to pay up. He did not, however, let her off the hook: “it’s unacceptable what she did.”

The rebuke marks a stunning fall from favor for a woman who, until recently, was among the most mulish loyalists in Trump’s orbit. Habba rose to prominence as the president’s personal attorney in 2021 and parlayed that into a short stint as counselor to the president. From there, she took the top job at the New Jersey US Attorney’s Office, which she left last December.

The news of her deal caps a dramatic few weeks for Habba. She wed Turkish billionaire Turhan Mildon on Sept. 26 at the Waldorf Astoria. One source pegged the cost of the bash at around $10 million, and FBI Director Kash Patel, Attorney General Todd Blanche and boxer Mike Tyson were among the guests.

Less than two weeks later, at an Oct. 9 Oval Office meeting, Habba accused Ric Grenell — the former executive director of the Kennedy Center — of failing to deposit $5.6 million her new husband had earmarked for the center. The money was allegedly part of a $17.6 million wire Mildon sent to Texas Armament & Technology, a defense software company, in May 2025.

Trump then foisted the matter onto White House Counsel Will Scharf.

Mildon’s lawyers have since produced a text in which Grenell allegedly promised Mildon access to the president. Axios later Axios later reported that the $17.6 million came not from Mildon but from the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s finance ministry.

Grenell has denied any wrongdoing and reportedly denied sending the text.

“Absurd. I’ve never asked for one cent to be sent somewhere else pretending it was for the Kennedy Center and I’ve never received any payment from him at all,” Grenell wrote on X.

President Trump tore into his former personal attorney Alina Habba on Saturday night, calling her reported $50 million contract with the family of a Venezuelan banker he later pardoned “totally obnoxious and outrageous.”

“I thought it was terrible,” Trump told reporters as he arrived at a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida, where he joked he had come dressed as himself.

The president said he told Habba he didn’t want her to be paid.

“You know, it’s one thing for a person to get paid legal fees or whatever. She’s a lawyer,” Trump said. “I thought it was totally obnoxious and outrageous, and it’s not acceptable. Not acceptable at all.”

The family of Julio Herrera Velutini guaranteed Habba more than $50 million over four years in exchange for serving as general counsel of Concord Partners, a family company registered just days before she signed on, the New York Times reported last week.

Herrera, a billionaire banker, once faced federal bribery charges. By August 2025, his case had been whittled down to a guilty plea on a single misdemeanor campaign finance violation instead.

The family put Habba on a princely retainer of $10 million a year, plus bonuses, according to the Times. The 42-year-old attorney teed the job up while she was still on the Justice Department’s payroll.

Habba was just two weeks into her new gig at Concord Partners when Trump pardoned her boss’ father.

The lawyer, for her part, insists the timing is pure happenstance.

“Any insinuation that my employment — all of which has been vetted and disclosed to the DOJ — had anything to do with securing a pardon is false,” Habba told the Times.

The White House has also denied any connection, the outlet reported.

Trump “erupted” when he learned of the contract, according to the Times, then told aides and allies that some of the money ought to find its way to his future presidential library or some other Trump-linked outfit.

On Saturday, the president said he didn’t necessarily expect Habba herself to pay up. He did not, however, let her off the hook: “it’s unacceptable what she did.”

The rebuke marks a stunning fall from favor for a woman who, until recently, was among the most mulish loyalists in Trump’s orbit. Habba rose to prominence as the president’s personal attorney in 2021 and parlayed that into a short stint as counselor to the president. From there, she took the top job at the New Jersey US Attorney’s Office, which she left last December.

The news of her deal caps a dramatic few weeks for Habba. She wed Turkish billionaire Turhan Mildon on Sept. 26 at the Waldorf Astoria. One source pegged the cost of the bash at around $10 million, and FBI Director Kash Patel, Attorney General Todd Blanche and boxer Mike Tyson were among the guests.

Less than two weeks later, at an Oct. 9 Oval Office meeting, Habba accused Ric Grenell — the former executive director of the Kennedy Center — of failing to deposit $5.6 million her new husband had earmarked for the center. The money was allegedly part of a $17.6 million wire Mildon sent to Texas Armament & Technology, a defense software company, in May 2025.

Trump then foisted the matter onto White House Counsel Will Scharf.

Mildon’s lawyers have since produced a text in which Grenell allegedly promised Mildon access to the president. Axios later Axios later reported that the $17.6 million came not from Mildon but from the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s finance ministry.

Grenell has denied any wrongdoing and reportedly denied sending the text.

“Absurd. I’ve never asked for one cent to be sent somewhere else pretending it was for the Kennedy Center and I’ve never received any payment from him at all,” Grenell wrote on X.
